entry.title: Byte Budget
entry.content:
pwn.college • Shellcoding Challenges

The length limit for the shellcode is only 0x12 = 18 bytes. Also, the first page of the shellcode is not writable. Therefore, we cannot have a full open/read/write . We will have to implement two stages. However, since the first page is not writable, and the stack is not executable by default, none of the obvious two-stage approaches work. This points us in the direction of SROP (Sigreturn Oriented Programming).

⚠️ Still Not Yet Solved End-to-End. There is an outline of our approach and a confirmed stage0. Stage2 is still under development.

# 1. Problem Mechanics

• Input is only 18 bytes long.
• The first page of the shellcode is not writable.
• The stack is not executable by default.

# 2. Failed Approaches

• Two-stage, reading stage2 back into the shellcode page: The first page was not writable. I could not write to it.
• Read stage2 onto the stack and jmp rsp : Stack was not executable. Jumping there caused a SIGSEGV.

# 3. Right Direction: SROP

18 bytes are not enough space to contain all the logic, and the pages were restricted in what they could be written to, so we use rt_sigreturn to restore all of our registers at once:

  1. An 18-byte stage0: read(0, rsp, 0x400) reads a fabricated sigreturn frame onto the stack;
  2. stage0 calls rt_sigreturn ;
  3. the fabricated frame configures our registers to call mprotect to make our shellcode/page either executable or writable;
  4. jump to the actual stage2;
  5. stage2 calls open/read/write on /flag .

stage0 template (fits within 18 bytes):

(The exact assembled bytes are intentionally omitted; the takeaway is the template — a sub-18-byte read(0, rsp, N) followed by rt_sigreturn .)

# 4. Status / To Do

  • stage0 is short enough (18 bytes), can read + call rt_sigreturn .
  • Incomplete: The specific values in our fabricated sigreturn frame ( rsp/rip/rdi/rsi/rdx/rax , mprotect args, page-aligned addresses) need to be mapped out relative to struct rt_sigframe / ucontext and connected to where stage2 wants to run.

# 5. Takeaways (to date)

  • Double constraint of page perms + limited size → SROP: When your shellcode page is not writable, your stack is not executable, and your byte budget is small, rt_sigreturn (syscall 15) is how you get to set "every register in one syscall" — typically to call mprotect and gain execute permission.
  • Shortest possible stage0 template: read(0,rsp,N) + rt_sigreturn , with our fake sigframe directly behind it on the stack — reachable within those 18 bytes.
  • More to do: offset values for the fake sigframe and alignment/jump for mprotect(addr & ~0xfff,len,7) .

# 6. Other things like this

  • another "first page not writable" self-modifying challenge: Syscall Shenanigans

entry.title: Pocket Payload
entry.content:
pwn.college · shellcoding challenges
the first stage will accept only 0xc = 12 Byte of shellcode into an RWX region (at the fixed address 0x28a42000 ). 12 bytes won’t be able to do the job for you → use a small stage1 to build a rop environment & then SROP to execute execve("cat", "/flag") .

# 1. Mechanics of the challenge

  • a total of 12 bytes of shellcode will be landed on a fixed RWX page at 0x28a42000 (that mapping isn’t randomized by PIE).
  • read the flag once you have executed.

# 2. Main idea

Use the 12 bytes as both stage1 + a gadget pool simultaneously: read a rop chain to the stack → ret into the chain → write to leak a stack address → read again to load an SROP frame → rt_sigreturn to control every register → execve .

12-Byte stage1 (tail instructions double as gadgets):

Since we have a fixed RWX address, we know what our gadget addresses are:

the chain:

  1. stage1 read(0, rsp, …) reads a rop chain to the stack, then enters it via ret .
  2. Rop: write(1, rsi, rdx) leaks stack contents -> derive current stack base.
  3. Rop: read(0, rsi, …) again to load SROP payload (full sigcontext).
  4. pop rax; ret -> rax=15, syscall; ret -> rt_sigreturn , with forged registers executing: execve("/run/dojo/bin/cat", ["/run/dojo/bin/cat", "/flag", NULL], NULL) .

# 3. Key points/pitfalls

  • stage1 tail is gadget set: 58 c3 , 5f c3 , 0f 05 c3 -- all three gadgets live within those same 12 bytes. There’s no dependency on external binary and no hunting for gadgets.
  • stack address recovery: after the write leak, real stack base = stack_base - 0xb0 (subtract a fixed offset from the leaked value). SROP frame involves cat/flag/argv addresses are all calculated off of this one.
  • SROP sets every register at once: rt_sigreturn (syscall 15), restores rax/rdi/rsi/rdx/rip from on-stack sigcontext assembles execve call directly bypasses "12 bytes can't lay out arguments to execve".

# 4. Takeaways

  • tiny stage1 = read + built-in gadgets: with stage1 located at a fixed RWX address, reuse pop;ret / syscall; ret at stage1 tail as rop pool -- 12 bytes enough bootstrap arbitrarily long rop.
  • leak -> SROP -> execve: without string available “/bin/sh” , SROP directly into execve(cat, [cat,/flag]) is simpler than laying out execve’s arguments , rt_sigreturn is lever “set every register with one syscall”.

# 5. Related

  • even tighter length limit (6 bytes) : Micro Menace
  • uses SROP to defeat page-permisson / length limits : Byte Budget

entry.title: Micro Menace
entry.content:
pwn.college · Shellcoding Challenges
The first-stage is only 0x06 = 6 Bytes (this shellcode area is RWX; 0x1000 in size). Given that there is no way to fit both a read + ret into the 6-byte buffer space, the exploit relies on exploiting the original state of the registers (at which point rax = 0 and rdx = shellcode page address ) to create a 6-byte read stager to pull the second stage back over this same page, followed by natural fall through to run the second stage at page+6 .

# 1. Mechanics of the problem

  • A 6-byte input landing on the RWX shellcode page.
  • Registers relevant to how the shellcode will start: rax = 0 (perfect for SYS_read), rdx = shellcode page address (also perfect for the buffer).

# 2. Strategy

Six-bytes is barely enough space to build a minimal "read" stager — because we don't need to initialize either of the two registers that we know are already initialized on the entry to the shellcode ( rax = 0 already and rdx = this page already).

xor edi,edi ; 31 ff rdi = 0 (stdin) 2B
push rdx ; 52 rsi = rdx = this page 1B
pop rsi ; 5e 1B
syscall ; 0f 05 read(0, page, ... ) 2B Total 6B

i.e., a read(0, shellcode_page, ...) , reading stage2 back over the first part of this page.

Passing control through natural fall through: Once syscall returns, execution will resume right at shellcode_page + 6 (next to the end of the first stage). We can therefore append six NOPs to stage2, so that when we actually pull the payload back over here it lands at +6 and gets executed:

stage2 = b'\\x90' * 6 + real_shellcode

Total: 6B stage1 -> read stage2 onto this page -> after syscall finishes executing, continue executing at page+6 -> execute cat("/flag"). .

# 3. Possible pitfalls & important considerations

  • Use all that you see useful about the entry registers: rax=0 (the syscall number for read ) and rdx=page_address (ready-for-use buffer) provide us with enough info to cut corners and save bytes — therefore it isn’t necessary to add any instructions to prepare these registers before they’re used in our stager (hence why we were able to keep everything inside a 6-byte limit).
  • There’s simply too little room for a ret: if we’d appended a c3 (a ret instruction), the stager would’ve taken seven bytes. So instead, use natural fall-through: once read has written to this page, execution will naturally flow from here directly to page+6 ; line-up the beginning of stage2 with six NOPs.
  • Check your assumptions about the initial registers through experimentation: Each challenge might have different starting register values; experimentally determine what rax/rdx are, etc. Don’t guess wrong based only on a particular low-order byte of one of those.

# 4. What we learned

  • Shortest stagers rely on “borrowed pre-initialized registers”: If we only have enough bytes for a single syscall, don’t spend even a single precious byte initializing any register you know will be available to us on entry into the shellcode ( rax = syscall number, rdx = usable buffer); Use every last byte of your budget creating the syscall.
  • Instead of jump/return, fall through: Don’t bother including the bytes for jmp/ret , but instead let read overwrite this page; Let execution automatically pick up after the stager; Make sure to include an equivalent number of NOPs at the beginning of stage2.
  • Compare to Pocket Payload: Twelve-bytes is sufficient to bootstrap ROP/SROP; But we only have enough space for a six-byte minimal read stager — i.e., there’s no space for a ret.

# 5. Related

  • Previous challenge (12 bytes, ROP+SROP): Pocket Payload

entry.title: Diverse Delivery
entry.content:
pwn.college · shellcoding challenges

A rather unusual restriction on this challenge was that every byte of the shell code had to be unique – i.e., no byte could appear twice in the input shell code (up to 256 bytes, with no duplicate bytes). Inevitably, a full open/read/write will include repeated bytes (e.g. 0x0f05 , 0x31c0 , 0x00 ) -> the solution therefore has to have Two stages: stage 1 is a loader (with all distinct bytes), which loads an unconstrained stage 2.

⚠️ stage 1→stage 2 handoff not yet solved end-to-end: the general method is recorded but the specifics of how stage 1 communicates with stage 2 still needs refinement.

# 1. Mechanics of the problem

There is only a single input checked by the filter for whether or not every byte in the input is unique. Every normal shell code has far too many repeating bytes and is immediately rejected.

# 2. Overall methodology

  • stage 1 (loader with distinct bytes): loads the second stage from stdin (which we know is not subject to the same constraints) using a simple read(0, stage2_addr, 0x400); jmp stage2_addr . Each possible output of stage 1 is created by brute-forcing the landing address offset of stage 2 and checking if the length of the set of possible outputs equals the total number of distinct output bytes.
  • stage 2 (normal shell code): is loaded into memory by stage 1 and can then perform standard open/read/write operations.
  • how do you create stage 1's bytes uniquely? brute force stage 2 landing address offset: try each generated version of stage 1, and choose the first one where len(set) == len .

Stage2 logic: open("/flag", 0) → read(fd, rsp, 0x100) → write(1, rsp, n) → exit(0) .

# 3. Status/work left to do

  • the overall method works fine: a unique-byte stage 1 gets through the filter → reads a normal stage 2.
  • have not yet obtained Flag: the brute force for creating a unique-bytes stage 1 + finding correct landing address for stage 1 + creating the correct stage1->stage2 transition (read-size + timing + alignment of target for jmp rsi ) will need to be verified in a debugger.

# 4. Lessons learned (so far)

  • Two stages due to unique byte constraint: since the filter only examines the first segment, turn that segment into a small "mover" with all-distinct bytes, and bring in the real payload after examination.
  • creating small loader with all-distinct bytes: use compressed setup with cdq / push-pop /single-byte instrs, and brute force the address offset such that the four bytes of mov esi,imm32 are never among those used elsewhere — treat "uniqueness" as a searchable constraint

entry.title: Clobbercode
entry.content:
pwn.college · shellcoding challenges
write shellcode that reads /flag , but before it runs the shellcode is tampered with: every other 10-byte run is overwritten with 0xcc ( int3 , a breakpoint trap). So the layout becomes keep 10 / clobber 10 / keep 10 / clobber 10 … . The fix: chunk + short-jump — each surviving block ends with eb 0a to hop over the clobbered region.

# 1. Mechanics of the problem

This is not an insertion — it is an overwrite of every other 10 bytes with 0xcc :

[ 0..9  keep ][ 10..19 -> cc ][ 20..29 keep ][ 30..39 -> cc ] ...

0xcc = int3 . The moment execution flow hits one, it traps (SIGTRAP). So the clobbered runs must never be executed.

# 2. Main idea

Cut the shellcode into 10-byte-aligned blocks. Each "keep" block holds:

  • the first 8 bytes: real instructions (pad with 90 NOP if short);
  • the last 2 bytes: eb 0a ( jmp +0x0a ) — jump over the next 10 bytes (the run that will be overwritten with cc ) and land on the next keep block.

Structure:

[ 8B instrs + eb0a ][ 10B garbage -> cc ][ 8B instrs + eb0a ][ 10B -> cc ] …

The last block carries the tail (no further jump needed).

Logic: open("/flag", 0) → read(fd, rsp, 0x7f) → write(1, rsp, n) → exit(0) .

Because you cannot know where the garbage runs land in memory, state is passed between blocks through registers (fd, buffer pointer, byte count) rather than absolute addresses.

# 3. Pitfalls / key points

  • 0xcc = int3: the clobbered runs are not code you can fall through — you must actively jump past every one of them.
  • The trick is the layout, not the instructions: deliberately stuff 10 bytes of filler after each valid block so the challenge's overwrite lands exactly on the filler; the real instructions always sit in a "keep" block.
  • Only 8 bytes of usable budget per block: split open/read/write into multiple ≤8-byte pieces and chain them with eb 0a , carrying state in registers across the boundary.

# 4. Takeaways

  • Beating a "periodic overwrite" = jump-based chunking: when you know the period and position of the tampering, slice the code into "safe slots" and end each slot by jumping over the bad slot. An eb XX short jump is the cheapest bridge (2 bytes).
  • Instruction splitting: one logical operation (e.g. open ) can span several 8-byte slots, relying on registers to carry state between them — the stack/registers are your natural cross-slot storage.

# 5. Related

  • byte-level constraint series: Ello Ackers · Diverse Delivery

entry.title: Ello Ackers
entry.content:
pwn.college · shellcoding challenges
write shellcode that reads /flag , but with a byte blacklist: the byte 0x48 (ascii char: ‘H’) cannot be used in the shellcode. The x86-64 REX.W prefix ( 0x48 ) is present at nearly all 64bit operations ( mov rdi, rsp , mov rbx, imm64 , etc.) → a naive amd64 shellcode will fail.

# 1. How this challenge works

The hint: this challenge requires that your shell code has no H bytes! — meaning we can’t use the byte 0x48 in our shellcode ( 0x48 is ASCII 'H' , not lowercase 'h' which is 0x68 ).

0x48 is the REX.W, and it shows up in most of your 64-bit instructions: mov rdi, rsp ( 48 89 e7 ), mov rsi, rsp ( 48 89 e6 ), mov rbx, imm64 ( 48 bb … ), etc. Therefore, we have to write shell code that completes open/read/write without ever emitting REX.W.

# 2. Ideas for avoiding REX.W

Two key tricks for not using 0x48 :

  • using push/pop instead of mov reg, rsp: push rsp; pop rdi ( 54 5f ), push rsp; pop rsi ( 54 5e ) — no REX.W
  • zeroing / small immediates via 32-bit ops: xor eax, eax ( 31 c0 ), mov al, imm ( b0 .. ), xor esi, esi ( 31 f6 ) — none contain 0x48 .

The whole logic, kept REX.W-free:

open("/flag", 0)          ; build "/flag\0" on the stack, then push rsp; pop rdi
read(fd, rsp, 0x7f)
write(1, rsp, bytes_read)

# 3. Pitfalls / key points

  • REX.W ( 0x48 ) is everywhere: any mov/add/... on a 64-bit rXX register carries it by default. Swap to the 32-bit equivalents (the high 32 bits are zero-extended for free) and use push/pop to move the stack pointer around — that avoids 0x48 entirely.
  • Writing /flag onto the stack without 0x48 : mov dword [rsp], "/fla" ( c7 04 24 .. ) + mov byte [rsp+4], 'g' ( c6 44 24 04 .. ) — neither encoding contains 0x48 .

# 4. Takeaways

  • General way to beat a byte blacklist: replace "the encoding of the instruction that contains the forbidden byte" with an equivalent sequence that encodes differently.
  • Toolbox for avoiding REX.W: push rsp / pop rdi (move the stack pointer), 32-bit arithmetic (auto zero-extends), xor r32, r32 to zero, mov al, imm to set the syscall number — together they let you write an almost purely 1-byte-prefix amd64 shellcode.

# 5. Related

  • next category (forbidden syscall bytes, self-modifying): Syscall Smuggler

entry.title: Syscall Shenanigans
entry.content:
pwn.college · shellcoding challenges
Same forbidden syscall bytes as Syscall Smuggler (0f 05 / 0f 34 / cd 80), but with one additional twist: Removing write access to the First 4096 bytes of shellcode. — the First page of the shellcode is read-only. therefore, you cannot modify the First page yourself; instead, place the pseudo-syscall Stub on the second page (offset > 0x1000, therefore writable), rewrite it to 0f 05 at run-time, and call rbx it from the First page.

# 1. Challenge mechanics

  • forbidden bytes: syscall = 0f 05 , sysenter = 0f 34 , interrupt = cd 80 .
  • the First page (0..0xfff) is read-only, so the previous challenge's "place 0f 04 in your code and increment it," will be a sigsegv due to the fact that the First page is read-only.

# 2. Conceptual idea

  • the main code resides on the First page (execute-only).
  • place the pseudo-syscall Stub 0e 04 c3 on the second page (padding after 0x1000) — the second page is writable.
  • at the beginning, lea rbx,[rip+disp] addresses the second-page Stub, then inc [rbx] / inc [rbx+1] writes 0e 04 to 0f 05 , thus making the Stub become syscall;ret .
  • afterward each syscall uses that Stub via call rbx .

Logic: open("/flag", 0) → read(fd,rsp,0x100) → write(1,rsp,n) → exit(0) , all use call rbx as their routing mechanism.

# 3. Obstacles / important points

  • First page is read/execute only and not writable, therefore, the Self-modification target must reside on a writable page (the second one). There are no other important differences here compared to smuggler.
  • use 0e 04 as pseudo bytes: two increments produce 0f 05 . Input includes none of 0f 05 or any other restricted Byte sequences (assure prior to transmitting).
  • call rbx reuses the Stub: saves bytes by having "the bytes being modified" located in a single location — modify once use many times.

# 4. Takeaways

  • modification under W^X: target page must be writable. When the First page is made readonly by the challenge, move "bytes to be modified" to another writable page; First page just executes lea + inc + call .
  • stubified system call: 0f 05 c3 as single writable "system call function", reusable via call ; both bypass filter and save space. It is a generic template for system call Byte restricted challenges.

# 5. Related

  • previous challenge (allowed to Self-modify on First page): Syscall Smuggler
  • non-writable First page & length limited: Byte Budget

entry.title: Syscall Smuggler
entry.content:
pwn.college · Shellcoding Challenges
Write shellcode that reads /flag , however the input may NOT include any of the following sequences of bytes related to system calls: syscall ( 0f 05 ), sysenter ( 0f 34 ), or int ( cd 80 ). The trick to get around this: self-modifying code, i.e., submit an input sequence that is very close to being a syscall sequence, and when run-time occurs +1 that into a true 0f 05 .

# 1. Mechanics of the problem

Input to the filter will pass as long as it does not have the machine code for syscall ( 0f 05 ) in it. Therefore the state of the input cannot have 0f 05 inside of it.

# 2. Main idea

Take advantage of the difference between what is being filtered on ("the static bytes") versus what runs ("the dynamic bytes"):

  • Put 0f 04 in your input (it is not a syscall, therefore it should pass the filter).
  • At the beginning of your shellcode, write inc byte ptr [rip+offset] . This adds one to the 04 , thus at run time it turns into 0f 05 .
  • Now that we've modified the original 0f 05 c3 ( syscall; ret ), we just need to follow it through to our patched version ( 0f 04 c3 -> 0f 05 c3 ).

Logic: open("/flag", 0) -> read(fd, rsp, 0x7f) -> write(1, rsp, 0x7f) , where each call to a syscall goes through that self modifed stub ( 0f 04 c3 -> 0f 05 c3 ).

# 3. Points to avoid / important details

  • Filter only looks at static input bytes, not dynamic bytes: therefore by splitting up 0f 05 into "0f 04" + a runtime inc , you are well within bounds of its inspection.
  • inc byte [rip+disp] ( fe 05 .. ) references the pseudo-syscall byte at the end of your pseudo-instruction, once it's been modified, either use call to jump back there, or simply continue to execute (after modifying).
  • There is no byte black list on this challenge so REX.W is allowed -- it employs mov rax, imm64 ( 48 b8 .. ) to fill in a reference to /flag . (Compare w/Ello Ackers where 0x48 was disallowed).

# 4. Takeaways

  • Shellcode which modifies itself: solution to a "static byte filter" -- submit a legitimate near miss and modify it into the forbidden instruction at run-time. inc / add / xor can all be employed to restore the target byte.
  • Reusable syscall stub: treat 0f 05 c3 as a small function you can call over and over again. It conserves space and limits the self modification to a single location.

# 5. Related

  • Previous category (byte blacklist): Ello Ackers
  • Following challenge (same syscall sequences + first page non-writeable): Syscall Shenanigans

entry.title: Jan 29 Master Method Cases, General Form of Divide and Conquer
entry.content:
# Three Master Method Cases

# General Form

The recurrence relation is given as:

T(n)=a⋅T(nb)+f(n)T(n) = a \cdot T\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) + f(n) T(n)=a⋅T(bn​)+f(n)

  • a>1a > 1a>1: number of subproblems
  • b>1b > 1b>1: factor by which the input size is divided
  • f(n)f(n)f(n): additional work outside the recursive calls
  • nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a: the threshold function

# Case #1: f(n)=O(nlog⁡ba−ϵ), ϵ>0f(n) = O\big(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon}\big), \, \epsilon > 0f(n)=O(nlogb​a−ϵ),ϵ>0

  • Condition: f(n)f(n)f(n) grows asymptotically slower than nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a.
  • Explanation: The additional work f(n)f(n)f(n) is dominated by the contribution from the recursive subproblems.
  • Result:

    T(n)=Θ(nlog⁡ba)T(n) = \Theta\big(n^{\log_b a}\big) T(n)=Θ(nlogb​a)

# Case #2: f(n)=Θ(nlog⁡ba)f(n) = \Theta\big(n^{\log_b a}\big)f(n)=Θ(nlogb​a)

  • Condition: f(n)f(n)f(n) grows at the same rate as nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a.
  • Explanation: The work from the recursive subproblems and the additional work f(n)f(n)f(n) contribute equally.
  • Result:

    T(n)=Θ(nlog⁡ba⋅log⁡n)T(n) = \Theta\big(n^{\log_b a} \cdot \log n\big) T(n)=Θ(nlogb​a⋅logn)

# Case #3: f(n)=Ω(nlog⁡ba+ϵ), ϵ>0f(n) = \Omega\big(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon}\big), \, \epsilon > 0f(n)=Ω(nlogb​a+ϵ),ϵ>0

  • Condition: f(n)f(n)f(n) grows asymptotically faster than nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a, but satisfies the regularity condition:

    a⋅f(nb)≤c⋅f(n),for some constant c<1.a \cdot f\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) \leq c \cdot f(n), \quad \text{for some constant } c < 1. a⋅f(bn​)≤c⋅f(n),for some constant c<1.

  • Explanation: The additional work f(n)f(n)f(n) dominates the contribution from the recursive subproblems.
  • Result:

    T(n)=Θ(f(n))T(n) = \Theta\big(f(n)\big) T(n)=Θ(f(n))

# Regularity Condition

For Case #3 to apply, the function f(n)f(n)f(n) must satisfy the regularity condition:

a⋅f(nb)≤c⋅f(n),for some constant c<1.a \cdot f\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) \leq c \cdot f(n), \quad \text{for some constant } c < 1. a⋅f(bn​)≤c⋅f(n),for some constant c<1.

This ensures f(n)f(n)f(n) is "smooth" enough to dominate nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a.

# Summary of Cases

Case Condition on f(n)f(n)f(n) Result for T(n)T(n)T(n)
Case 1 f(n)=O(nlog⁡ba−ϵ)f(n) = O\big(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon}\big)f(n)=O(nlogb​a−ϵ) Θ(nlog⁡ba)\Theta\big(n^{\log_b a}\big)Θ(nlogb​a)
Case 2 f(n)=Θ(nlog⁡ba)f(n) = \Theta\big(n^{\log_b a}\big)f(n)=Θ(nlogb​a) Θ(nlog⁡ba⋅log⁡n)\Theta\big(n^{\log_b a} \cdot \log n\big)Θ(nlogb​a⋅logn)
Case 3 f(n)=Ω(nlog⁡ba+ϵ)f(n) = \Omega\big(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon}\big)f(n)=Ω(nlogb​a+ϵ) and satisfies the regularity condition Θ(f(n))\Theta\big(f(n)\big)Θ(f(n))

These cases comprehensively determine the growth rate of the recurrence based on f(n)f(n)f(n).

# General Framework for Divide-and-Conquer

  1. Identify how to divide the problem into smaller sub-problems.
  2. Determine the base case (when the problem size is small, how to solve it).
  3. Figure out how to combine the result of sub-problems.

# Example: Maximum Sum Subarray Problem

Input: A[1…n]A[1 \dots n]A[1…n] (an array of integers).
Output: A subarray A[i…j]A[i \dots j]A[i…j] such that 1≤i≤j≤n1 \leq i \leq j \leq n1≤i≤j≤n and: sum(i,j)=∑k=ijA[k]\text{sum}(i, j) = \sum_{k=i}^j A[k]sum(i,j)=∑k=ij​A[k] is maximized.

# Example Array:

A = [3, -4, 5, -2, -2, 6, -3, 5, -3, 2]
For the subarray A[3…8]A[3 \dots 8]A[3…8]:

sum(3,8)=5+(−2)+(−2)+6+(−3)+5=9\text{sum}(3, 8) = 5 + (-2) + (-2) + 6 + (-3) + 5 = 9 sum(3,8)=5+(−2)+(−2)+6+(−3)+5=9

# Algorithm A: Brute-Force Algorithm

  • Steps:

Time Complexity: Θ(n2)\Theta(n^2)Θ(n2)

# Algorithm B: Divide-and-Conquer

  • Steps:

    1. Divide the array into two halves.
    2. Solve for the left half and the right half recursively.
    3. Combine the results to find the maximum subarray crossing the middle.

  • Example Array Division:
    A = [3, -4, 5, -2, -2, 6, -3, 5, -3, 2]
    Divide into:

  • Left: [3,−4,5,−2,−2][3, -4, 5, -2, -2][3,−4,5,−2,−2], result: 555

  • Right: [6,−3,5,−3,2][6, -3, 5, -3, 2][6,−3,5,−3,2], result: 888

  • Time Complexity: Θ(nlog⁡n)\Theta(n \log n)Θ(nlogn)

# Algorithm C: Dynamic Programming (Kadane's Algorithm)

  • Steps:

    • Maintain a running sum for the current subarray.
    • Reset the sum to 0 if it becomes negative, and track the maximum sum so far.

  • Time Complexity: Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n)

entry.title: Jan 27 Three ways of Solving Recurrence Equations
entry.content:
# Three ways of Solving Recurrence Equations

# Recursion tree

  • Recursion Tree means to keep expanding the recurrence equation by replacing its left-hand side by right hand side until reaching the base case.

# Here is a typical form of Recurrence Equation:

T(n)=T(n2)+T(n4)+nT(n)=T(\frac{n}{2})+T(\frac{n}{4})+nT(n)=T(2n​)+T(4n​)+n

# Equation Explanation

  • T(n)T(n)T(n) is the time complexity of the algorithm.
  • When the problem has a size nnn, it is divided into two subproblems: one of size n2\frac{n}{2}2n​​ and another of size n4\frac{n}{4}4n​​. The time required to solve these subproblems is T(n2)T(\frac{n}{2})T(2n​) and T(n4)T(\frac{n}{4})T(4n​), respectively.
  • Apart from solving the subproblems, the algorithm performs an additional amount of work proportional to nnn, which could involve merging, sorting, or some other operations.
  • The recursion continues by breaking the subproblems further until a base case is reached, usually when n=1n=1n=1 or a very small size.

# Recursion tree of T(n)=T(n2)+T(n4)+nT(n)=T(\frac{n}{2})+T(\frac{n}{4})+nT(n)=T(2n​)+T(4n​)+n

    0   1   2 ...... [levels]
T(n)
├── T(n/2)
│   ├── T(n/4)
│   │   ├── T(n/8)
│   │   ├── T(n/16)
│   │   └── n/16
│   ├── T(n/8)
│   │   ├── T(n/16)
│   │   └── n/16
│   └── n/2
├── T(n/4)
│   ├── T(n/8)
│   │   ├── T(n/16)
│   │   └── n/16
│   ├── T(n/8)
│   │   ├── T(n/16)
│   │   └── n/8
│   └── n/4
└── n

According to the graph above, the total work amount(or time, for algorithm) for each level would be:

  • level 0: nnn
  • level 1: 34∗n\frac{3}{4}*n43​∗n
  • level 2: 916∗n\frac{9}{16}*n169​∗n
  • .......
  • level xxx: (34)x∗n(\frac{3}{4})^{x}*n(43​)x∗n

# Total working time would be:

T(n)=(34)0∗n+(34)1∗n+...(34)k∗n=n⋅{(34)0+(34)1+⋯+(34)k}T(n)=(\frac{3}{4})^0*n+(\frac{3}{4})^1*n+...(\frac{3}{4})^k*n= n \cdot \left\{ \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^0 + \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^1 + \cdots + \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^k \right\} T(n)=(43​)0∗n+(43​)1∗n+...(43​)k∗n=n⋅{(43​)0+(43​)1+⋯+(43​)k}

# Worst-case:

k=log⁡2nk = \log_2 n k=log2​n

# Best-case:

k=log⁡4nk = \log_4 n k=log4​n

Check text book page. 1168, Geometric series for further explanation of Worst-case / Best-case solution.

# Substation method

# Recurrence Equation Example:

T(n)=T(n)+1T(n) = T(\sqrt{n}) + 1T(n)=T(n​)+1

# Substation method Steps:

  1. Guess a solution first.
  2. Use mathematical induction to prove your guess is correct.
  3. Trial-and-error.

# Derivation

  1. Start with:
    T(n) = T(\sqrt{n}) + 1 \tag{\#0}
  2. Let k=log⁡2n  ⟹  n=2kk = \log_2 n \implies n = 2^{k}k=log2​n⟹n=2k
  3. Define S(k)=T(n)=T(2k)S(k) = T(n) = T(2^k)S(k)=T(n)=T(2k):
    S\left(\frac{k}{2}\right) = T\left(2^{k/2}\right) \tag{\#1}
  4. From #0, substitute:
    S(k) = T(n) = T(\sqrt{n}) + 1 = T(2^{k/2}) + 1 = S\left(\frac{k}{2}\right) + 1 \tag{\#2}
  5. Recurrence relation for S(k):
    S(k) = S\left(\frac{k}{2}\right) + 1 \tag{\#3}

# Recurrence Tree

  • Expand S(k) as a recursion tree:
  • Each level contributes a constant 1 to the total.
  • Total levels of recursion:

L=log⁡2k=log⁡2(log⁡2n)L = \log_2 k = \log_2 (\log_2 n) L=log2​k=log2​(log2​n)

# Solution

  1. From the recursion tree:
    T(n)=Θ(log⁡2(log⁡2n))T(n) = \Theta(\log_2 (\log_2 n))T(n)=Θ(log2​(log2​n))
  2. Using S(k)=T(n)S(k) = T(n)S(k)=T(n):
    T(n)=Θ(log⁡2(log⁡2n))T(n) = \Theta(\log_2 (\log_2 n))T(n)=Θ(log2​(log2​n))

# Summary Table

Contribution S(k/2^i) + 1 Total contribution per level Levels
S(k) 1 -
S(k/2) 1 0
S(k/4) 1 1
... ... ...
S(1) 1 L=log⁡2kL=\log_2 kL=log2​k

The total work accumulates across log⁡2k\log_2 klog2​k levels, resulting in T(n)=Θ(log⁡2(log⁡2n))T(n) = \Theta(\log_2 (\log_2 n))T(n)=Θ(log2​(log2​n)).

# Master's method

# Definition of Master's method:

  • Master method is a "cook book" for solving one type of recurrence equation

T(n)=a∗T(nb)+f(n)(a≥1,b>1)T(n)=a*T(\frac{n}{b})+f(n) (a≥1, b>1) T(n)=a∗T(bn​)+f(n)(a≥1,b>1)

  • Change the original problem size nnn into a(a≥1)a (a≥1)a(a≥1) sub-problems, each of equal size (nb)(b>1)(\frac{n}{b})(b>1)(bn​)(b>1)

# Limitations of Master's method:

  • If f(n)f(n)f(n) is non-polynomial function, such as exponential, then master's method can't be applied
    • Exclusion Example: T(n)=T(n2)+2nT(n)=T(\frac{n}{2})+2^{n}T(n)=T(2n​)+2n
  • If f(n)f(n)f(n) is monotone functions, such as sin(n)sin(n)sin(n),cos(n)cos(n)cos(n), then master's method can't be applied.
    • Exclusion Example: T(n)=2∗T(n4)+sin(n)T(n)=2*T(\frac{n}{4})+sin(n)T(n)=2∗T(4n​)+sin(n)
  • Special form of master's method
    • Exclusion Example: T(n)=a∗T(nb)+θ(nklog⁡pn)T(n)=a*T(\frac{n}{b})+\theta(n^{k}\log^{p}n)T(n)=a∗T(bn​)+θ(nklogpn)
      In this class, you're NOT allowed to use above to solve a recurrence equation

# Application:

# Always compare two functions:

nlogban^{log_{b} a}nlogb​a and f(n)f(n)f(n)

# General conclusion:

  • Which ever function is an upper bound of another one, that function becomes tight bound for T(n)T(n)T(n). If the two functions have exactly the same growth rate, then T(n)=θ(f(n)∗logn)=θ(nlogba∗log2n)T(n)=\theta(f(n)*log n)=\theta(n^{log_{b}a}*log_{2}n)T(n)=θ(f(n)∗logn)=θ(nlogb​a∗log2​n)

# Case #1: nlog⁡ba>f(n)n^{\log_b a} > f(n)nlogb​a>f(n)

  • f(n)=O(nlog⁡ba−ϵ)(ϵ>0)f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon}) \quad (\epsilon > 0)f(n)=O(nlogb​a−ϵ)(ϵ>0)

    • nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a is an upper bound of f(n)f(n)f(n).
    • nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a is only larger than f(n)f(n)f(n) by a constant polynomial factor.

  • Then:

    T(n)=Θ(nlog⁡ba)T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) T(n)=Θ(nlogb​a)

# Case #2: nlog⁡ba=f(n)n^{\log_b a} = f(n)nlogb​a=f(n)

  • nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a and f(n)f(n)f(n) have the same growth rate.

  • Then:

    T(n)=Θ(f(n)⋅log⁡n)=Θ(nlog⁡ba⋅log⁡n)T(n) = \Theta(f(n) \cdot \log n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \cdot \log n) T(n)=Θ(f(n)⋅logn)=Θ(nlogb​a⋅logn)

# Case #3: nlog⁡ba<f(n)n^{\log_b a} < f(n)nlogb​a<f(n)

  • nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a is a lower bound of f(n)f(n)f(n).

  • f(n)=Ω(nlog⁡ba+ϵ)(ϵ>0)f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon}) \quad (\epsilon > 0)f(n)=Ω(nlogb​a+ϵ)(ϵ>0)

    • f(n)f(n)f(n) is only larger in a constant polynomial factor than nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a.

  • Then:

    T(n)=Θ(f(n))T(n) = \Theta(f(n)) T(n)=Θ(f(n))

# Additional Note

  • "Regularity Rule": The conditions above assume that f(n)f(n)f(n) satisfies certain regularity properties, such as being polynomialy larger or smaller than nlog⁡ban^{\log_b a}nlogb​a.

entry.title: Jan 22 Algorithms Design
entry.content:
# Algorithms Design

# There are three major techniques of designing algorithms:

# 1. Divide-and-Conquer

  1. Divide: change/divide the original problem into sub-problems
  2. Conquer: if the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly
  3. Combine: combine the solutions of sub-problems into solution to the original problem

# Example: Merge Sort Algorithm

Merge-Sort(A, p, r) // A[p...r]
    if p == r then
        // Base case: array has only one element, no need to sort.
        return
    else
        q = (p + r) / 2 // Find the middle index
        Merge-Sort(A, p, q)     // Recursively sort the left half
        Merge-Sort(A, q + 1, r) // Recursively sort the right half
        Merge(A, p, q, r)       // Merge the sorted halves

Merge(A, p, q, r)
    // Step 1: Calculate the sizes of the two halves
    n1 = q - p + 1            // Size of the left half
    n2 = r - q                // Size of the right half

    // Step 2: Create temporary arrays for the left and right halves
    Let L[1..n1 + 1] and R[1..n2 + 1] be two new subarrays

    // Step 3: Copy data into the temporary arrays
    for i = 1 to n1 do
        L[i] = A[p + i - 1]   // Copy left half into L
    for j = 1 to n2 do
        R[j] = A[q + j]       // Copy right half into R

    // Step 4: Add sentinel values (∞) to signal the end of the arrays
    L[n1 + 1] = ∞
    R[n2 + 1] = ∞

    // Step 5: Merge the two sorted subarrays back into A[p...r]
    i = 1
    j = 1
    for k = p to r do
        if L[i] ≤ R[j] then
            A[k] = L[i]
            i = i + 1
        else
            A[k] = R[j]
            j = j + 1

# Recurrence Equation:

  • When an algorithm contains a recursive call to itself, we use ∼ to describe the overall running time of the problem in terms of the running time of smaller size sub-problems.
  • These kinds of equation is called as "got ~"
  • Using "Merge Sort" as an example:
    • T(n)=T(n2)+T(n2)+Θ(n)=2∗T(n2)+Θ(n)T(n) = T(\frac{n}{2}) + T(\frac{n}{2}) + \Theta(n) = 2*T(\frac{n}{2}) + \Theta(n)T(n)=T(2n​)+T(2n​)+Θ(n)=2∗T(2n​)+Θ(n)
    • T(n)=T(n2)+T(n2)+Θ(n)=2∗T(n2)+Θ(n)T(n) = T(\frac{n}{2}) + T(\frac{n}{2}) + \Theta(n) = 2* T(\frac{n}{2}) + \Theta(n)T(n)=T(2n​)+T(2n​)+Θ(n)=2∗T(2n​)+Θ(n)

# Example: Quick Sort Algorithm

QuickSort(A, p, r)
    if p >= r
        // Base case: do nothing
        return
    else
        q = Partition(A, p, r) // Partition the array and get the pivot index
        QuickSort(A, p, q - 1) // Recursively sort the left sub-array
        QuickSort(A, q + 1, r) // Recursively sort the right sub-array

Partition(A, p, r)
    x = A[r]       // Pivot is the last element
    i = p - 1      // Initialize the partition index

    for j = p to r - 1
        if A[j] ≤ x
            i = i + 1
            Swap A[i] with A[j] // Move smaller elements to the left

    Swap A[i + 1] with A[r]     // Place pivot at its correct position
    return i + 1                // Return the pivot index

  • Array: A=[2,8,7,1,3,5,6,4]

  • Quick Sort steps:

    1. Keep moving j to the right until finding the first element ≤ x, j stops.
    2. when j stops, i moves one position to its right
    3. swap elements at index i with element at index j
    4. continue the three steps above until j == r-1

  • The key idea of Partition is to divide the original array into serval areas

  • Recurrence equation for Quick Sort

    1. Worst-case: T(n)=T(1)+T(n−1)+Θ(n)T(n) = T(1) + T(n - 1) + \Theta(n)T(n)=T(1)+T(n−1)+Θ(n)
    2. Best-case:T(n)=T(n2)+T(n2)+Θ(n)=2∗T(n2)+Θ(n)T(n) = T(\frac{n}{2}) + T(\frac{n}{2}) + \Theta(n) = 2 *T(\frac{n}{2}) + \Theta(n)T(n)=T(2n​)+T(2n​)+Θ(n)=2∗T(2n​)+Θ(n)
    3. General-case ("Randomized Partition"):
      • Randomly generate an integer ( i ) between ( 1 ) to ( n ).
      • Use ( A[i] ) as pivot to do the partition.

    Recurrence relation here:

    T(n)=T(n16)+T(15n16)+Θ(n)T(n) = T\left(\frac{n}{16}\right) + T\left(\frac{15n}{16}\right) + \Theta(n) T(n)=T(16n​)+T(1615n​)+Θ(n)

entry.title: Jan 13 Linked List Review
entry.content:
# Linked List Structure:

head -> [data | next] -> [data | next] -> NULL

# Linked List Insertion:

# When we are trying to insert a new node, there are 3 special cases:

  1. Empty linked list
    • head == NULL
  2. Trying to insert the head node (non-empty list)
  3. Trying to insert the last node (non-empty list)

After eliminating these three special conditions, a common insertion was performed.

# Linked List Deletion:

# There are two special cases we need to consider when deleting nodes of a linked list:

  1. The list is empty
  2. After the deletion, the list is empty

Sample Code from Canvas

// ASU CSE310 Sample Code
// Description: This program displays a simple LinkedList with nodes.

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

// A LinkedList Node contains a data and a pointer that points to the next Node
struct Node
{
    int data;
    Node *next;
};
  
// A simple LinkedList class demo
class LinkedList
{
private:
    Node *head; // always points to the first Node of the list. Do NOT remove it.
  
public:
    // constructor. Initialize an empty linked list
    LinkedList()
    {
        head = NULL;
    }
  
    // LinkedList insertion demo. This function will always insert a new
    // Node at the head of the linked list
	void insertNodeAtFront(int n)
    {
        // create a new Node
        Node *aNewNode = new Node;
        aNewNode->data = n;
        aNewNode->next = NULL;
  
        // if it is an empty linked list, insert it as the first node
        if (head == NULL)
            head = aNewNode;
        else
        {
            aNewNode->next = head;
            head = aNewNode;
        }
    } // end of insertNodeAtFront
  
    // LinkedList deletion demo. This function will delete the last node
    void deleteLastNode()
    {
        // if it is an empty linked list, cannot delete
        if (head == NULL)
            cout << "Empty linked list, deletion error" << endl;
        else if (head->next == NULL) // linked list contains only one node
        {
            delete head;
            head = NULL;
        }
        else
        {
            // we will use two pointers for the deletion
            Node *current = head;
            Node *previous = NULL;
  
            // traverse through the linked list to the end
            while (current->next != NULL)
            {
                previous = current;
                current = current->next;
            }
            // after above while loop, current points to the last node
            delete current;
            previous->next = NULL;
            current = previous;
        }
    } // end of deleteLastNode()

    // this function prints Linked list contents from head to tail
    void printList()
    {
        Node *temp = head;
        if (head == NULL)
            cout << "Empty linked list" << endl;
        else
        {
            while (temp != NULL)
            {
                cout << temp->data << ", ";
                temp = temp->next;
            }
            cout << endl;
        }
    } // end of printList
}; // end of class LinkedList definition
  
// driver function used to test/check above linked list
int main()
{
    LinkedList sampleList; // create an LinkedList object
  
    int num;
  
    // sentinel value controlled while loop that allows user to continue
    // inserting a Node until 0 is entered
    cout << "Enter an integer (enter 0 to stop): ";
    cin >> num;
  
    while (num != 0)
    {
        sampleList.insertNodeAtFront(num);
        cout << "\nEnter an integer (enter 0 to stop): ";
        cin >> num;
    }
    sampleList.printList();
    sampleList.deleteLastNode();
    sampleList.deleteLastNode();
    sampleList.printList();
}

entry.title: Jan 15 Algorithms Analysis
entry.content:
# Algorithmic Analysis

# Analytical Aspects:

  1. Time Complexity (Focused aspects)
  2. Space Complexity

# Analytical Method:

  1. count the total number of execution steps
  2. count the maximum number of steps for the worst-case

# Example: Insertion Sort Algorithm

For the worst case, the list needed to be sorted should starts with the biggest element, and descending to the smallest element:

Initial Case:

1 2 ... n-2 n-1 n
n n-1 ... 3 2 1

After one insertion (1 comparison, 1 shift)

1 2 ... n-2 n-1 n
n-1 n ... 3 2 1

After one insertion (2 comparisons, 2 shifts)

1 2 ... n-3 n-2 n-1 n
n-2 n-1 n ... 3 2 1

...and so on

  • the nth insertion need n-1 comparisons and n-1 shifts
  • Time complexity: 2⋅∑i=1ni=2⋅n(n+1)2=n(n+1)2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^n i = 2 \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = n(n+1)2⋅∑i=1n​i=2⋅2n(n+1)​=n(n+1)

# Asymptotic Notations

# Big-O Notation ("upper bound", worst-case scenario)

  • This is the most used notation
  • used to express the maximum number of steps

# Example:

  • Given two functions

    • f(n)f(n)f(n)
    • g(n)g(n)g(n)

  • denote f(n)=O(g(n))f(n)=O(g(n))f(n)=O(g(n)) (f(n)f(n)f(n) has an upper bound of g(n)g(n)g(n))

  • iff there exists positive constants n0n_0n0​ and c, such that:

    • 0≤f(n)≤c∗g(n)0≤f(n)≤c*g(n)0≤f(n)≤c∗g(n) for all n≥n0n≥n_0n≥n0​

# Big-Ω Notation ("lower bound", best-case scenario)

  • This is used to express the minimum number of steps

# Example:

  • Given two functions

    • f(n)f(n)f(n)
    • g(n)g(n)g(n)

  • denote f(n)=Ω(g(n))f(n)=Ω(g(n))f(n)=Ω(g(n)) (f(n)f(n)f(n) has an lower bound of g(n)g(n)g(n))

  • iff there exists positive constants n0n_0n0​ and c, such that:

    • 0≤c∗g(n)≤f(n)0≤c*g(n)≤f(n)0≤c∗g(n)≤f(n) for all n≥n0n≥n_0n≥n0​

# Big-Θ Notation ("tight bound")

  • Two function only differ in constant factor

# Example:

  • Given two functions
    • f(n)f(n)f(n)
    • g(n)g(n)g(n)
  • denote f(n)=Θ(g(n))f(n)=Θ(g(n))f(n)=Θ(g(n)) (f(n)f(n)f(n) has an tight bound of g(n)g(n)g(n))
  • iff f(n)=O(g(n)f(n)=O(g(n)f(n)=O(g(n) and f(n)=Ω(g(n)f(n)=Ω(g(n)f(n)=Ω(g(n), such that:
    • f(n)=Θ(g(n)f(n)=Θ(g(n)f(n)=Θ(g(n)

# Efficiency of Algorithms

  • Given problem P, let's assume we get two algorithms. A and B.
  • A is more efficient than B iff A's worst-case running time has a lower "order of growth" than B's.

# Order of Growth Chart:

Function Expression Type Description Rank
f1(n)=400f_1(n) = 400f1​(n)=400 Constant Constant function 1 (slowest)
f2(n)=log⁡2nf_2(n) = \log_2 nf2​(n)=log2​n Logarithmic Logarithmic growth 2
f3(n)=2nf_3(n) = 2nf3​(n)=2n Linear Linear growth 3
f4(n)=n2+2nf_4(n) = n^2 + 2nf4​(n)=n2+2n Polynomial Polynomial growth 4
f5(n)=2nf_5(n) = 2^nf5​(n)=2n Exponential Exponential growth 5
f6(n)=n!f_6(n) = n!f6​(n)=n! Factorial Factorial growth 6 (fastest)

# !! In practice, only algorithms run in Polynomial Time or Less is acceptable/efficient

# !! In terms of "order of growth", slower is better since it takes less number of steps to solve the problem

entry.title: 1 Linux Basics
entry.content:
# Linux:

  • an operating system with a GUI interface

# Command line and Terminal

  • most interaction is done via a terminal
  • a terminal is a program used to interact with the shell
  • the shell enables access to the operating system
  • Terminal, command line, shell and any specific shells
    • basically referring to the same thing

# Shells

  • Windows shells
    • command prompt
    • PowerShell
  • Linus shells
    • Bash (Born Again shell)
    • also other shells, but works similar
    • example: uname@~/app/1

# File system

  • no hard drives, such as C:\
  • everything starts from / the root directory

# Path

  • Path is the list of / separated directory names

# Absolute path

  • absolute path starts with a /
  • list all the directories separated by a /
  • /home/code/app/1/data

# Relative path

  • relative path starts from the current directory
  • may include a slash after first character
  • app/1/data

# Two relative path operators

  • single dot .
    • current directory
  • double dot ..
    • 1 directory up the chain

# cd: Navigating directories

  • cd is short for change directory, it changes your working directory
  • cd works with absolute and relative paths
  • if type cd only, will go to the home directory

# ls: Listing directories

  • lists the files and directories within this directory
  • common flags -la
  • Bash shortcut, ll = ls -la
  • File/Directory pattern matching
    • * Wild card - 0 to any number of any character
      • ls * list all files
      • ls *.c lists all files that end in .c
    • ? Wild card for a single character
      • ls file?.c
      • lists file1.c filea.c file3.c......

# mkdir: Creating directories

  • make directory

# mv

# Moving files or directories

  • mv: mv <source> <target>

# Renaming files

  • mv: mv <oldname> <newname>

# cp: Copying files or directories

  • cp: cp <file> <target>

# rm: Removing a file or directory

  • rm: rm <file>
  • -i
    • prompt the user for each deletion
  • -v
    • with specific information
  • *
    • Remove everything that is not a directory
    • does not start with a period
  • -r
    • Remove everything except items starting with period in current directory

# echo: Print the value provided

  • by defaule, includes a new line \n at the end

# cat: Quickly looking at file contents

  • prints the contents of a file to the terminal

# grep: Search and return

  • grep: means global regular expression
  • searches a pattern and returns the line that match
    • grep <option> <pattern> [file]

# Running programs

  • Running a program from the command line requires
    • the path to the program
    • Any arguments sent into the program
  • While it runs the program
    • Outputs to standard output (terminal in most cases)
    • Takes input via standard input (keyboard in most cases)
  • Returns a code on exit
    • uname@~/app/1 $ /bin/false
    • uname@~/app/1 $ /bin/echo "$?"
    • 1 (this is the value returned from /bin/false )
  • Must use ./ to execute a program in out current directory

# Redirection

# Redirecting I/O

  • Default standard

    • Input:
      • standard input- keyboard input
    • Output
      • standard output with a file descriptor of 1
      • standard error with a file descriptor if 2

  • can redirect a file to be any of these

  • use < to redirects input of the target to the provided device or file

    • Input less than expected can cause errors
    • Redirects to standard input

  • Example:

    • test.input contains "Erik"
  • use > to redirect output from a program to a file
  • use | to pipe one output to another input

or

# Regular Expressions

  • Regular expressions (regex) are sequences of characters that define search patterns

  • Used for string matching, validation, and text processing

  • Basic characters

    • Literals: meow
    • The Wildcard .
    • Square Brackets \[a-zA-Z]

  • Quantifiers

    • Come after a literal character, wildcard character, or square brackets
    • describes how many times the proceeding item will occur
      • Asterisk * matches 0 or more occurrences
      • Braces {n,m} Matches between n and m occurrences

  • Example Regex Patterns:

    • Email Validation:
      • [a-zA-Z0-9._%+!]*@[a-zA-Z0-9._%+!]*
      • matches any email address
    • Phone Number:
      • ([0-9]{3})[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}
      • (123)456-7890

# Misc

# gcc: Compile C source code

  • gcc : compiles C source to a binary executable
  • -o is where to put the binary executable

entry.title: Rainworld
entry.content:
# 中文版:

终于通关了《雨世界》，经历了各种艰难，查阅攻略才完成。这款游戏虽已问世七年，但以现在的标准来看，无论在美术、玩法、机制还是剧情上都达到了极高的水准，是我心目中制作最精良的 2D 游戏之一。


《雨世界》是一款基于 Unity 引擎制作的 2D 独立游戏。在游戏中，玩家扮演一种被称为 “蛞蝓猫” 的生物，在古代文明遗留下的废墟中探索生存。乍一看似乎是传统的探索类 RPG，但制作组在美术和机制上的精细打磨，使其脱颖而出。


首先是美术方面。玩家在控制蛞蝓猫时，会穿越古文明的废墟，随处可见裸露的钢筋架、断裂的管道和通风系统，彰显了曾经的文明辉煌。然而，这一切又被层层植被覆盖，形成了一个繁盛的生态系统。废墟的 “破败” 与新生命的 “生机” 相互交织，又形成鲜明的对比。



这种感觉在蛞蝓猫进入古代遗迹、仍在勉强运作的巨大结构中达到顶峰。游戏中的 “迭代器” 内部，广阔的 “系统总线” 宛如八车道高速公路，而神经元组件则如同深海中的荧光鱼群，又似星辰在无重力场中漂浮。古文明的宏伟与蛞蝓猫的渺小对比鲜明，让人既震撼又惋惜。



在机制方面，制作组赋予《雨世界》每种生物不同的 AI，并使用类似 3D 骨骼绑定技术制作所有动物。这让游戏中的生物不仅具有基本的 “战或逃” 反应，还具备一定的思考和判断能力。结合流畅自然的动作，构建了一个栩栩如生、完整的生态系统。这种生态还原程度，即使在以生态系统为卖点的游戏中也十分罕见。



生命在古代废墟中焕发，渺小的蛞蝓猫在其中穿行。冷却水自迭代器中排出，如瀑布般的大雨冲刷着新生的生命。这正是我喜爱《雨世界》的原因：抛开剧情对轮回与虚无主义的探讨，化身食物链低端的蛞蝓猫，在这个精心构建的世界中游荡，细细感受曾经与现在的一切，这本身就是一种极大的美好。

图片参考 b 站视频 BV1gg4y1d7oj

# English Version:

Finally, I have completed Rain World after going through countless difficulties, and I had to rely on guides to make it through. Though this game has been out for seven years, by today's standards, whether in terms of art, gameplay, mechanics, or story, it still stands at an impressively high level. In my opinion, it’s one of the most exquisitely crafted 2D games ever made.


Rain World is a 2D indie game made using the Unity engine. In the game, players take on the role of a creature known as the "Slugcat," exploring and surviving in the ruins left behind by an ancient civilization. At first glance, it may seem like a traditional exploration RPG, but the development team's meticulous polishing of both the art and mechanics sets it apart from the rest.


Starting with the art, as the player controls the Slugcat, they traverse the ruins of an ancient civilization. Exposed steel structures, broken pipes, and ventilation systems are visible everywhere, showcasing the glory of a once-great civilization. Yet, all of this is overgrown with layers of vegetation, creating a flourishing ecosystem. The contrast between the "decay" of the ruins and the "vitality" of new life intertwines, forming a striking juxtaposition.



This feeling reaches its peak when the Slugcat enters the still-operational massive structures of the ancient ruins. Inside the game’s "Iterators," the vast "system buses" resemble eight-lane highways, while neuron components appear like glowing schools of fish in the deep sea, or stars drifting in a zero-gravity field. The grandeur of the ancient civilization stands in stark contrast to the small Slugcat, evoking both awe and regret.



On the mechanics side, the development team gave each creature in Rain World its own AI, utilizing a technology similar to 3D skeleton rigging to animate all animals. This means the creatures in the game not only have basic "fight or flight" reactions but also possess a certain level of thinking and decision-making ability. Combined with smooth and natural movements, this builds a vivid and complete ecosystem. The level of ecological simulation here is rare, even among games that specifically market their ecosystems as key features.



Life thrives within the ancient ruins as the tiny Slugcat roams through it. Cooling water is discharged from the Iterators, with torrential rains washing over newly born life. This is why I love Rain World—setting aside the story's exploration of the themes of reincarnation and nihilism, simply becoming a low-level creature in the food chain, wandering through this meticulously crafted world and slowly feeling everything from the past and the present, is an immense beauty in itself.
